stemMd: According to the passage, why can a pedestrian feel hotter on a pale street than on a dark one?

options.label: A
options.textMd: The pale paving is itself hotter than dark asphalt.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Pale paving stores heat and releases it in the evening.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Dust and soot on pale paving absorb the sunlight.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Streets with pale paving usually have fewer trees.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Sunlight reflected by the paving strikes people and walls.

explanationMd:
Find the sentence about pale pavements; it is at the end of the third paragraph, and it gives the cause directly: the sunlight they reflect "does not disappear but strikes passers-by and the walls of nearby buildings". The reflected light, not the ground, is what warms the pedestrian.

The same sentence rules out the most tempting wrong answer: the pedestrian feels hotter "even though the ground beneath is cooler", so the pale surface is not the hotter one. Storing heat and releasing it in the evening is what the first paragraph says about dark asphalt, the opposite case. Dust and soot are mentioned only as reducing the effect of roof coatings, and trees are mentioned only in the first paragraph, about cities in general.

distractorRationale.a: The passage says the pedestrian feels hotter "even though the ground beneath is cooler". The pale surface is the cooler one.
distractorRationale.b: Storing sunlight and giving it back through the evening is what the first paragraph says about asphalt and dark roofing, not about pale paving.
distractorRationale.c: Dust and soot are mentioned as reducing the effect of a reflective roof coating. The passage does not use them to explain why pale streets feel hot.
distractorRationale.d: Trees come up only in the first paragraph, as a general cause of city heat. Nothing links pale streets to having fewer trees.

accessibilityText: A stated-information question about the reflective roofs passage. It asks why a pedestrian can feel hotter on a pale street than on a dark one. The five choices: The pale paving is itself hotter than dark asphalt; Pale paving stores heat and releases it in the evening; Dust and soot on pale paving absorb the sunlight; Streets with pale paving usually have fewer trees; Sunlight reflected by the paving strikes people and walls.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank against an original passage; it tests locating a stated cause and resisting choices that borrow details from elsewhere in the passage. Every option is answerable, or refutable, from the passage text alone.
